title: How the price responds
objectives: Read delta, gamma, vega and theta from how an option’s price curve moves.
Give the sign of each for long and short calls and puts, and size a delta hedge.

screens.prose: A call struck at £100.00 with six months left, rates at 0. The curve is its price now; the bold line is its payoff at expiry. The short straight line touches the curve at the share price, and its label is its slope.
screens.question: Slide the share from £80.00 to £120.00. What happens to the slope?

options.text: It rises smoothly from near 0 towards 1
It jumps from 0 to 1 at the strike
options.why: That is the payoff's slope, the bold line. The curve has no kink, so its slope changes smoothly.

options.text: It stays at 1: the call moves one for one with the share
options.why: Slide to £80.00 and read the label. Far below the strike the call barely moves.

options.text: It falls as the share rises
options.why: Read the label at £80.00 and again at £120.00. It grows.

feedback.correct: From about 0.07 at £80.00 to about 0.91 at £120.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the label at £80.00, at £100.00 and at £120.00.

explain.text: Far below the strike the call is unlikely to pay, so it hardly moves. Far above, it behaves almost like the share less the strike. In between, the slope climbs smoothly.

screens.prose: That slope is **delta**: how much the option's price moves for each £1.00 move in the share, for small moves. The share is at £100.00, where the label reads 0.53.
screens.question: The share rises from £100.00 to £102.00. About how much does the call gain?

hints.text: Delta is the gain per £1.00 on the share.
The share moves £2.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply delta by the share's move.

byKey.one-for-one: You moved the call one for one with the share. It moves by delta, 0.53, per pound.
byKey.per-pound: That is the gain for a £1.00 move. The share moved £2.00.

explain.text: The change is about $\Delta \times 2.00 = 0.53 \times 2.00 = 1.06$. The curve bends, so for big moves the straight line is only a first guess. Slide to £102.00: the slope there is already higher.

screens.prose: Delta itself changes as the share moves. Slide £10.00 at a time and note the label: £80.00, £90.00, £100.00, £110.00, £120.00.
screens.question: Over which £10.00 range does delta change the most?

options.text: Near the strike, from £90.00 to £100.00 or £100.00 to £110.00
Deep in the money, from £110.00 to £120.00
options.why: Above £110.00 the curve is nearly straight, so its slope settles near 1.

options.text: Far out of the money, from £80.00 to £90.00
options.why: From £80.00 to £90.00 delta rises from 0.07 to 0.25. Near the strike it rises by more.

options.text: The same over every range
options.why: Then the curve would be a parabola. Read the labels: the steps are uneven.

hints.text: Write down the five deltas.
They read about 0.07, 0.25, 0.53, 0.77 and 0.91.
The steps are 0.18, 0.28, 0.24 and 0.14. The biggest are either side of £100.00.

feedback.correct: Near the strike: the curve bends most there.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take each delta from the next, and compare the steps.

explain.text: Delta steps up by 0.28 and 0.24 either side of the strike, but only 0.14 from £110.00 to £120.00. How fast delta changes is **gamma**, the curve's bend. It is largest near the strike.

screens.prose: Now a put struck at £100.00, six months, rates at 0. Its curve falls as the share rises. Slide the share and read the slope.
screens.question: What is the put's delta with the share at £100.00?

hints.text: Slide to £100.00 and read the label.
A falling curve has a negative slope.
The label reads −0.47.

feedback.correct: −0.47: the put loses about 47p for each £1.00 rise in the share.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the share to £100.00 and read the slope, sign included.

byKey.sign: You dropped the sign. The put's curve falls as the share rises, so its slope is negative.
byKey.call: That is the call's delta. The put's slope at £100.00 is negative.

explain.text: The put's delta is $-0.47$, between $-1$ and 0. Note that $0.53 - (-0.47) = 1$: the call's delta less the put's is exactly 1. We derive why below.

screens.prose: Volatility is how much the share tends to move. The two curves are the same call, six months to expiry, priced at 20% and at 40% volatility.
screens.question: What does the rise in volatility do to the call's price?

options.text: It raises the price at every share price, most near the strike
It lowers the price: more risk makes the call less attractive
options.why: You treated risk as bad for the holder. A call's loss is capped at its price, so bigger moves only add to its upside.

options.text: It raises the price only where the call is out of the money
options.why: Look at £100.00: the price almost doubles, from £5.64 to £11.25.

options.text: It raises the payoff at expiry too
options.why: The payoff at expiry is fixed by the strike. Volatility changes only the price before expiry.

hints.text: Compare the two curves at £100.00 and at £120.00.
At £100.00 the price goes from £5.64 to £11.25.
The 40% curve is above the 20% curve everywhere, with the widest gap near £100.00.

feedback.correct: Higher volatility lifts the whole curve, most near the strike.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two curves at several share prices.

explain.text: The shift up when volatility rises is **vega**. Bigger moves help the holder above the strike, and the floor at 0 caps the harm below. So long options have positive vega, largest near the strike.

screens.prose: The same call at 20% volatility, priced with six months left and with five weeks (0.1 years) left. Nothing else has changed: just time passing.
screens.question: With the share at £100.00, how much value does the call lose as six months shrink to five weeks?

hints.text: Read both curves at £100.00.
The two points are labelled.

feedback.correct: £3.12. As expiry nears, the curve sinks towards the payoff.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the five-week price from the six-month price at £100.00.

byKey.sum: You added the two prices. The loss is the gap between them.
byKey.ratio: You divided the prices. The loss is in pounds: the difference.

explain.text: The loss of value as time passes is **theta**, negative for a long option. Less time means less chance of a big move, so less insurance. Near the strike the curve sinks fastest; far from it there was little time value to lose.

screens.prose: Back to one curve, with the share at £110.00. Slide the time left towards 0 and watch the curve and the slope.
screens.question: Just before expiry, what is the call's delta at £110.00, and what would it be at £90.00?

options.text: 0.5 at both: the share is as likely to rise as to fall
options.why: You treated delta as a coin toss. With almost no time left the call at £110.00 is all but certain to pay $S - 100$.

options.text: About 0.77 at £110.00, as with six months left
options.why: Slide the years left down to 0.01. The slope moves away from 0.77 as the curve hugs the payoff.
You swapped them. The payoff's slope is 1 above the strike and 0 below it.

hints.text: What does the curve become at expiry?
As time runs out the curve settles onto the bold payoff line.
The payoff's slope is 1 above the strike and 0 below it.

feedback.correct: At expiry the price is the payoff, so delta is 1 in the money and 0 out of it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the years left to 0.01 and read the slope.

explain.text: With no time left the curve is the payoff, so delta is 1 above the strike and 0 below. Deep in the money it is near 1 even before expiry: the option moves one for one with the share. Gamma piles up at the strike as expiry nears.

screens.prose: A colleague reads the at-the-money call's delta of 0.53 and says: the call has a 53% chance of finishing in the money.
screens.question: What is wrong with her reading?

options.text: Delta is a slope, a hedge ratio. It is close to a probability, but not the same thing
Nothing: delta is the chance of finishing in the money
options.why: You read the slope as a chance. In the standard model the in-the-money chance used for pricing is 0.47 here, not 0.53, and the real-world chance differs again.

options.text: Nothing, because at the money every chance is 50%
options.why: You assumed a 50% chance at the money. Delta is 0.53 and the pricing chance is 0.47; neither is exactly a half.

options.text: The chance is $1 - 0.53 = 0.47$, so she has it backwards
options.why: 0.47 happens to be the model's pricing chance here, but not because of $1 - \Delta$. That is the put's delta in size.

hints.text: What did we measure on the canvas?
Delta is the tangent's slope.
A slope says how the price moves. Under the standard model the chance used for pricing is a different number, 0.47 here.

feedback.correct: Delta is a sensitivity. Read it as how many shares hedge the option.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what delta measures on the curve.

byKey.right: You treated the slope as a probability. They are close for a call under some assumptions, but delta is 0.53 here and the model's chance 0.47.
byKey.half: You used 50% at the money. Rates, volatility and time move both numbers away from a half.

explain.text: In the standard model, $\Delta = N(d_1) = 0.53$ but the pricing chance of finishing in the money is $N(d_2) = 0.47$. Real-world chances depend on the share's expected return, which neither uses. A related slip: theta is not a loss you avoid by waiting; it is the price of the insurance.

screens.prose: Collect what we have read. A short position is the long one with every sign flipped. Type + or − in each cell.
screens.question: Fill in the sign of each Greek for each position.

hints.text: Delta: does the position gain when the share rises?
Both long options gain from bigger moves and lose as time passes.
Long call: + + + −. Long put: − + + −. Flip every sign for the short positions.

feedback.correct: Long options: positive gamma and vega, negative theta. Short options: the reverse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill the long rows first, then flip every sign for the short rows.

byKey.r1c1: A put loses as the share rises, so its delta is negative.
byKey.r1c2: A put's curve bends upwards too, so a long put has positive gamma.
byKey.r2c4: A short call earns the decay the holder loses, so its theta is positive.
byKey.r3c1: A short put gains when the share rises, since the put loses value.

explain.text: Only delta tells calls from puts. Gamma, vega and theta depend only on long or short. A long option buys movement and pays for it in time decay; the writer is paid for time and hurt by movement.

screens.prose: We saw $0.53 - (-0.47) = 1$. Parity from l9 explains it, for European options on a share with no dividend.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Raise $S_0$ by a small amount: the right side rises by the same amount, as $K/(1+r)^T$ does not move
So $c - p$ rises by that amount too: $\Delta_c - \Delta_p = 1$

hints.text: Start from parity.
Ask how each side moves when the share moves.
Parity, the right side's move, the left side's move, then solve for $\Delta_p$.

feedback.correct: The call and put deltas always differ by exactly 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with parity, then move the share.

byKey.c: The left side's move follows from the right side's. Put the line about the right side first.
byKey.d: Solving for $\Delta_p$ is the last step.

explain.text: Parity holds at every share price, so its two sides have equal slopes. The right side has slope 1. With $\Delta_c = 0.53$ that gives $\Delta_p = -0.47$, as we read off the put's curve.

screens.prose: A market maker has sold 1,000 calls on a share, each on one share, and wants no exposure to small moves. Each call's delta is 0.6.
screens.question: How many shares must the market maker buy to be delta neutral?

hints.text: The short calls lose about how much per £1.00 rise in the share?
1,000 calls times 0.6 is a delta of −600.
Each share has delta 1, so 600 shares cancel −600.

feedback.correct: 600 shares. Short 1,000 calls at 0.6 is a delta of −600.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number of calls by delta, then cancel it with shares.

byKey.full: You hedged one share per call. Each call moves only 0.6 as much as a share.
byKey.sell: You sold shares. Short calls lose when the share rises, so the hedge must gain then: buy.
byKey.rest: You used $1 - 0.6$. The calls' delta is 0.6 each, so buy 0.6 shares per call.

explain.text: A £1.00 rise costs the calls about £600.00 and earns the 600 shares £600.00. After a big jump, though, delta rises: short calls have negative gamma, so the hedge falls short and must be topped up at the higher price. That is how gamma hurts the short side.

```python

```

ideas: Before expiry an option's price is a smooth curve above its payoff. **Delta** is its slope: about 0 far out of the money, about 1 deep in, and $\Delta_p = \Delta_c - 1$.
**Gamma** is how fast delta changes, largest near the strike. **Vega** lifts the curve when volatility rises. **Theta** sinks it as expiry nears.
Long options have positive gamma and vega and negative theta; short options the reverse. A delta hedge holds $n\Delta$ shares against $n$ options.

formula.name: Delta, read from the curve
formula.note: At expiry the curve is the payoff, so a call's delta is 1 above the strike and 0 below.

summary.trap: Delta is a slope and a hedge ratio, not the chance of finishing in the money. Theta is the cost of the insurance, not a loss to dodge.

quiz.prose: A trader sold calls and holds shares to be delta neutral. Overnight the share jumps 10%.
quiz.question: What happens to her position?

options.text: It loses: the calls' delta rose, so her shares no longer cover them
Nothing: delta neutral means no exposure to any move
options.why: Delta neutral covers small moves. A jump changes delta, and short calls have negative gamma.

options.text: It gains: the shares rose 10%
options.why: The shares gain, but the short calls lose more, as their delta climbs during the jump.

options.text: It gains from higher volatility
options.why: A short call has negative vega. If volatility rises, she loses on that too.

feedback.correct: Negative gamma: big moves hurt the short side.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the jump does to the calls' delta.

explain.text: As the share rises, the calls' delta rises, so each further pound costs her more than her shares earn. A big move either way loses money for a short-gamma book. She is paid theta for carrying that risk.

quiz.prose: Two calls on the same share, struck at £100.00, with the share at £100.00. One has a year left, the other a week.
quiz.question: Which is true?

options.text: The one-year call costs more
The one-week call costs more: it will pay sooner
options.why: Paying sooner is not worth more here. Less time means less chance of a big move, so less value.

options.text: They cost the same: the payoff is the same
options.why: The payoff is the same, but the price before expiry includes time value.

options.text: The one-week call is worthless: it is not in the money
options.why: An at-the-money call with a week left can still finish in the money. It is cheap, not worthless.

feedback.correct: More time, more value, for a long option on a share with no dividend.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what time gives the holder.

explain.text: Time gives the share room to move above the strike. As expiry nears that room shrinks, which is theta. At the strike the one-week call keeps only a little time value.
